coherence.reasons: Both run a clean hierarchy from a 'do not launch, grow software' governing thought through market, unit economics, pop-up, cash and alternative. X is tighter: four summary claims map one-to-one onto slides. Its one wobble is the slide 6 title ('at best break even') sitting over a −$1.76 result that only reaches −$0.08 with a promotion cut no site has shown. Y's question tree maps sub-questions to sections and every section claim carries page references. Its wobble is lifting a heavily assumption-laden estimate ($13.7M acquisition bill) into the executive summary. Neither has a real break in logic.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (decline, fund software, sell store-based fast delivery, set re-entry triggers). Y weighs the trade-offs more fully. It tests the recommended software path against the investors' own objectives: break-even at about $11M ARR, cash of $5.4M at end 2028 at 60% growth, and a breach of the floor at 30% growth. It names that as the biggest risk and lists three risks of saying no with mitigations. X asserts the runway rule is 'Kept' on the software path without checking it, and says 'waiting costs us little' without weighing the downside. X does better on the Zipcart pricing alternative, showing it turns positive at best-observed inputs and adding a service-fee test as a trigger. That is not enough to offset Y's stress-testing of its own recommendation.

evidence.reasons: Both hit every required calculation: −$6.17, −$1.76, −$12.57, +$2.02, $2.5M or about six months of runway, and roughly 42% growth. X's extra figures check out (−$0.08 with a 2% promotion rate, +$0.22 to +$1.52 when one input falls back to best observed, 3.75 orders per rider-hour, −$1.05 and +$3.97 with Zipcart's levers). Its slips are small: it says pricing 'works only alongside best-ever order value and density' when best density alone would suffice, and the 'Kept' runway claim is unsupported. Y adds correct break-evens ($63.4 order value, 14.4 orders per rider-hour, −$0.48 and −$1.05 for Zipcart, $7.1 an hour rider pay). It has one small error: the plan without the order-value gain loses about $0.73, not $0.30. It also leans on two speculative extrapolations: the $13.7M acquisition bill ('before any store opens') and a software model that holds costs flat while ARR grows 2.5 times. Both are flagged, but both carry headline claims. Y never shows that Zipcart's fee turns positive at best density, so it uses that evidence one-sidedly. X is slightly cleaner.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis on the right grounds: growth is real but separate from profit, every observed input set loses money, the pop-up's growth was bought with promotions, and the runway floor breaks even on plan. Both avoid the 'launch one city to prove density' trap and move learning to customer sites. X treats the part of the evidence that supports the founders more even-handedly. It shows Zipcart's levers would turn positive at best-observed inputs (+$3.97) but not at the median (−$1.05), calls pricing 'the only lever with evidence behind it', and makes a fee test a trigger for reopening. Y frames Zipcart mainly as a rebuttal, though it gives both median figures and credits the founders on growth.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, correct and defensible. X is the sharper, more economical case against the launch and handles the Zipcart counter-evidence more evenly. Y gives the board more of what it needs to decide: it tests the alternative against the investors' profitability and runway constraints with a downside case, sets out the risks of saying no, and adds break-even sensitivities showing that no single lever, including density, can rescue a median store. Y's extra extrapolations are speculative but flagged and do not change the answer. Y serves the decision maker slightly better.
